## Why FAM217B is in the study

In the UC study highlighted by the presentation, **FAM217B promoter hypermethylation coincided with lower RNA expression**. The panel was discovered on 450K arrays in 8 UC and 3 control tissues and technically validated in a larger UC series [Kang et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5000688/).

The primary study used 3 normal controls and 8 UC tissues for array discovery, then methylation-specific PCR and bisulfite sequencing in 79 UC samples. FAM217B was one of three promoters selected for validation, and bulk qRT-PCR supported lower transcript abundance [@kang2016ucpanel]. This is discovery-plus-technical-validation evidence, not an independent diagnostic validation cohort, and the design did not resolve cell composition.

## What does it do?

The scientifically important answer is: **its human function is not established**. [NCBI Gene](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/63939) classifies it as protein coding and places the product in cytosol and nucleoplasm; curated pathway-level mechanism is lacking. “Family with sequence similarity” is a naming placeholder, not a functional description.

## What happens if expression stops?

No credible colon-specific loss-of-function mechanism can currently be asserted. Silencing could be biologically consequential, neutral, a marker of altered cell composition, or a passenger of inflammatory chromatin remodeling. The correct experiment is to confirm methylation–RNA–protein coupling in defined cell types and perturb the gene in an appropriate epithelial model.

## Biomarker status

FAM217B is presently more defensible as a candidate *state marker* than as a mechanistic driver. A useful next study would preregister CpGs and thresholds, include inflammation-matched non-UC controls, validate in an external cohort, and report whether the marker adds information beyond histology, medication, age, and epithelial fraction.

<details><summary><strong>What would move the mechanism forward?</strong></summary>

Single-cell localization, CRISPRi/CRISPR knockout, rescue, epithelial barrier phenotyping, and replicated tissue–plasma methylation are more informative than pathway guesses based on the name.
</details>
